summary: This unit teaches you to manage the finances of a department or cost centre within an approved budget: understanding your budget, spending limits and authority, recording orders and spending, working out and explaining variances, forecasting the year end, taking corrective action, handling transfers (virements), contingencies and emergencies, following procurement and ethics rules, reporting to senior managers and reviewing the year. It is written for supervisors and managers in Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Most supervisors and managers do not set the organisation's budget, but they are **given a budget and held responsible for staying within it**. This unit teaches you to do that: to know your budget, to record and monitor every dollar committed and spent, to explain differences, to act early when spending drifts, and to report honestly.
**Who it is for:** supervisors, officers and managers who are budget holders in businesses, hotels, schools, health centres, municipal corporations, ministries and agencies.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Understand your budget and your authority
Know what each budget line covers, how it is phased by month, your spending limit and who approves above it.
Keep your own log of orders (commitments) and actual spending, and reconcile it with finance's reports.
Calculate variances and percentages, tell favourable from adverse, separate timing differences, price and volume effects, and use a flexed budget.
Project the outturn from spending so far and reforecast during the year.
Find the cause, decide what you can control, and act without harming essential services.
Use virements and contingency under the rules, and manage unbudgeted costs after events such as storms.
Keep to spending limits and procurement rules, avoid order splitting, declare gifts, and seek value for money.
Report to senior managers, delegate smaller budgets safely, and review the year to improve the next budget.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions and sums on variances, percentages, forecasts and flexed budgets.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as virement, commitments, outturn) and longer answers on controlling and reporting.
**Group practical tasks**: a spending log reconciled with a finance report with a variance report, and a role-played budget review meeting with a corrective plan. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by two different routes. A budget report with a wrong figure loses your director's trust faster than an overspend.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Your budget, your authority and your role

terms: Budget
An approved plan of expected income and spending for a period, usually a year, in money terms.
Cost centre
A department or unit whose costs are recorded together, such as maintenance, stores or the front office.
Budget holder
The manager who is accountable for spending within a cost centre's budget and limits.
Budget line
One item of the budget, such as overtime, supplies, repairs, utilities or training.
Phasing
Spreading the yearly budget over months, according to when costs are expected to fall.
Spending limit (authority limit)
The highest amount a person may approve on his or her own signature.
Delegated authority
Authority given to a person lower down for stated amounts and purposes.

blocks.h: What a new budget holder should do first

flow: Get the approved budget and read each line, with its assumptions (for example, 'overtime based on 600 hours a quarter')
Find out how it is **phased by month**: some costs fall in the same months every year, such as insurance premiums or school-term costs
Confirm your **spending limit** and who approves above it
Agree with finance how and when reports are issued, and how costs are coded
Set up your own **spending log** and calendar of large purchases

blocks.p: Organisations set a limit for each level of manager so that **each decision is taken at the right level of authority**. If a supervisor may approve up to J$150,000 and needs equipment worth J$210,000, she does not sign it herself. She sends it to the manager whose limit covers J$210,000.

blocks.note: Splitting one purchase into several smaller orders to stay under your limit is a **control breach**, even if the total cost is reasonable. It defeats the purpose of the limit and may be treated as misconduct.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A budget is phased because money is not needed evenly. A hotel's costs may rise before the winter season; a school's before term opens. Plan large purchases against the phasing and the organisation's **cash position**, so that budget and cash are available when each cost falls due.

blocks.note: Being within the yearly budget is not enough. If the whole year's money is spent in six months, you are in trouble in the second half. Always compare spending with the **budget to date**.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Finance sends monthly reports, but you are accountable. **Keep your own record** so that you can check finance's figures and spot errors early.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Costs already incurred and recorded (invoices paid or posted)
Orders placed or contracts signed but not yet invoiced or paid. The money is **promised**

blocks.p: Track commitments as well as actual spending because **money already promised is not free to spend again**. A report that shows only invoices will tell you that you are fine until the invoices arrive.

blocks.h: What a good spending log contains

ul: date, supplier, description, purchase order number, amount, budget line
committed amount and actual amount (and the date invoiced and paid)
running total by line and the balance available
reference to approval where needed

flow: Compare your totals line by line with the finance report
List every difference: an invoice not yet posted, a cost on the wrong line, an amount entered wrongly, a duplicate
Check the source documents (invoice, purchase order, receiving note)
Report errors to finance in writing and ask for correction
Keep a note of the agreement and check it in the next report

blocks.p: If your log shows J$1,020,000 for the quarter and finance shows J$1,065,000, **compare the items line by line** and find the J$45,000 difference. Do not assume either is right. An overspend on a line where nothing was bought is often a **coding error**: a cost put on the wrong budget line.

head: Budget size
Suggested review
rows: Actual against budget **each month**, with reasons for variances, and a weekly check of commitments
Monthly review of the finance report and your log
Any budget at a risk point
Before each large purchase, and at each quarter and the year end

blocks.note: Online access to the finance system is a great help because **problems can be spotted and acted on early**. Do not wait for the printed monthly report.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **variance** is the difference between the budget and the actual figure. For costs, **actual below budget is favourable, actual above budget is adverse**.

**Variance = budget − actual** (for a cost, a positive answer means under budget). The table below shows the size of each variance, and the last column gives its direction. **Variance % = variance ÷ budget × 100.** Say clearly whether it is favourable or adverse.

blocks.note: Always use the **budget** as the base for the percentage: 90,000 ÷ 600,000 = 15%. Not 90,000 ÷ 690,000.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Compare actual with the **phased** budget to date, not the whole year. A stationery budget of J$240,000, phased evenly, is J$20,000 a month. After six months the budget to date is J$120,000. If J$150,000 has been spent, the position is **J$30,000 over the budget to date**, even though only 62.5% of the year's total has been used.

The **outturn** is the expected final result for the year, estimated part-way through. A simple method: **spending so far ÷ months passed × 12**, adjusted for known changes. After nine months, J$2,700,000 spent on a J$3,300,000 budget means J$300,000 a month, so the full-year forecast is J$3,600,000, which is **J$300,000 over budget**. A **reforecast** is a fresh year-end estimate prepared during the year using actual spending to date and known future changes.

A **timing difference** appears when a cost is paid or posted in a different month from the plan, for example an invoice that has not yet arrived. The variance **reverses** later. Do not treat it as a real saving; check commitments.

An original budget is set for a planned level of activity. If activity is higher or lower, variable costs should change too. A **flexed budget** adjusts the variable costs to the actual level of activity, so you judge performance fairly.

**Example:** a hotel allows J$150 of cleaning supplies per occupied room. The plan was for 4,000 occupied rooms (a budget of J$600,000). If 4,600 rooms were occupied, the **flexed budget** is 4,600 × J$150 = J$690,000. Actual spend of J$680,000 is J$10,000 **under** the flexed budget, even though it is J$80,000 over the original budget.
A cost can be higher because **the price paid** was higher, or **the quantity used** was higher, or both.

ul: **Price variance** = (budgeted price − actual price) × actual quantity. If 2,000 litres were budgeted at J$200 and bought at J$230, the price variance is 30 × 2,000 = J$60,000 adverse.
**Usage variance** = (budgeted quantity − actual quantity) × budgeted price.

blocks.p: Price variances are often outside a manager's control (a supplier increase, the exchange rate). Usage variances are usually **within** it.

Organisations set a rule for which variances must be investigated, for example: any variance above 5% of the line or J$50,000, whichever is **lower**. On a J$300,000 line, 5% is J$15,000, so a J$24,000 variance must be investigated.

head: Colour
Meaning
rows: At risk: a variance is building and needs watching
Well off budget: needs action now

blocks.p: Use RAG with a **short note**: cause, effect, action. Colour alone does not explain anything.

A budget can be underspent and still be badly used. Measures such as **cost per trainee who completes a course**, cost per unit produced or cost per call handled show whether money is used efficiently.
If sales volume is 15% above plan and ingredient spending is 12% above budget, the extra spending is mostly explained by activity and is not alarming. Spending should be read against activity.

flow: Check the figures: coding errors, missing invoices, timing differences
Separate **controllable** from **non-controllable** causes (for example, overtime caused by your own rostering is controllable; a national price rise is not)
Find the **driver**: price, quantity, vacancy, one-off event, poor planning, weak control
Decide the action, its cost, effect on service and who owns it
Tell your director with the forecast and your plan
Check the result next month

head: Problem
Likely cause
Sound response
rows: Overtime 20% over budget because two posts are vacant
Fill or cover the vacancies and review the rota
Get new quotes, reduce waste (needless printing) and report the effect
Underspend of 70% on training at month nine
Reschedule courses, or report the saving. Risk: skills fall behind and goals are missed
Utilities over every month, stationery under
Use the finding to set more realistic lines next year

blocks.p: When cash is short, or you must save money, **rank spending by need**: protect safety, legal duties and essential services; delay non-urgent items; cut the lowest-value items first. For example, to save J$500,000 in the last quarter without harming service, list planned spending, score it by need and impact, and cut from the bottom.
**As soon as you see it**. If you see in July that the department will overspend by year end, tell your director in July, with the forecast and your plan, not in November when options are gone.

blocks.h: A good monthly report to senior management

ul: one page, figures checked
budget, actual, variance and percentage for each line and in total
an outturn forecast
each variance above the threshold with its **cause** and the **action**, owner and date
commitments and any risk
RAG rating

blocks.p: Staff make many small spending decisions every day. Share the targets, explain why they matter, show monthly results, **invite cost-saving ideas** and give credit. Cost control then becomes a team habit instead of the manager's fight.

blocks.h: Delegating a small budget to a team leader

blocks.p: Delegation brings decisions closer to the work and develops people. The risks are mistakes, poor records and breaches. Give the team leader **clear limits, a simple log and regular check-ins**, and keep overall accountability yourself. You remain accountable for the whole budget.

A **virement** is an approved transfer of budget from one line to another. Savings on the security contract can pay for urgent roof repairs **only** if the transfer is approved under the organisation's rules, for example by the finance manager or board. You may not simply spend a saving on another line. In many public bodies, virement between certain categories needs the approval of a higher authority.

blocks.note: Record the reason, the amounts, the approval and the date. A virement made without approval is a breach of financial rules.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **contingency** is a small sum set aside in the budget for costs that **could not be foreseen**. It is used under agreed approval rules, not to cover poor planning or routine costs.

flow: Make the site safe first: protect people, then property
Record the damage with photographs, dates and lists (needed for insurance and approvals)
Tell your director and finance at once, with a first estimate
Get quotes (follow emergency procurement rules, which still require records and approvals)
Check insurance and whether a claim is possible; notify the insurer in time
Seek approval for funding: contingency, virement or supplementary budget, with the reasons recorded
Track the extra cost separately and report it

blocks.p: If a budget holder has money left in February and the financial year ends in March, staff may say 'let us buy something or we lose it'. **Do not buy what you do not need.** Spend only on real needs, report the saving, and explain it. Wasteful spending damages trust; a saving is a good result. If the unused money is needed next year, ask, with reasons, but do not spend it to hide an unused budget.

If a department buys goods priced in US dollars, and the Jamaican dollar weakens, the J$ cost of the same goods **rises**. If the budget assumed J$150 to US$1 and the actual rate was J$156, a US$8,000 purchase budgeted at J$1,200,000 costs J$1,248,000, an adverse variance of J$48,000 (4%), with no change in quantity. Report it as a price effect outside the manager's control, and consider buying earlier, or quoting in J$ where possible.

blocks.note: Never assume an exchange rate in a sum: use the figures given. This unit does not require you to know the current rate.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Controls, ethics and value for money

blocks.p: The person who orders should not be the only person who receives, pays and records. Where two people check each other, errors and fraud are easier to find. Keep orders, receipts, approvals and payments traceable: purchase order, **receiving note**, invoice, **three-way match**, payment.

**Value for money** means the best mix of **cost, quality and useful life**, not simply the lowest price. A manager who buys from the cheapest bidder and finds the goods fail in a month has not obtained value for money. Compare whole-life cost: price, running costs, maintenance, expected life and support.

Public bodies must follow the **procurement rules for public bodies**, whose general aims are **fairness, openness, accountability, a recorded process and value for money**. A ministry manager may not award a cleaning contract to a favourite firm without quotes, even if it has done good work before. Use the quotation or tender route that fits the value; record why the winner was chosen.

blocks.h: Ethical risks for a budget holder

head: Risk
What to do
rows: Pressure to get round the rules (splitting an order, coding a cost to the wrong line to hide an overspend)
Refuse. Use the proper approval route. Report pressure.
Gifts or hospitality from suppliers (for example a free hotel weekend in return for renewing a contract)
Decline and report under the gifts policy.
Conflict of interest (a supplier owned by a relative)
Declare it and step out of the decision.
Using the organisation's money or assets for private ends
Never. Report if you see it.
Inflating forecasts to pad next year's budget
Be honest. A false forecast destroys credibility.

blocks.note: A budget holder controls money that belongs to the organisation or the public. Honesty, records and approvals protect both the money and you.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: In both, the manager keeps within the approved budget, monitors variances and reports honestly. In a private firm, owners or the board can often move money more freely if it improves profit. In a government agency the money comes from public funds, approved by Parliament or the responsible authority, and the manager answers to the public and to audit. Rules on transfers, procurement and reporting are stricter, and the fact of spending within the approved purpose matters as much as the amount.

flow: Compare final actual spending with budget for each line and in total
List the main variances and their causes
Separate **controllable** from **external** causes (price rises, exchange rate, storms)
Look for patterns across the year, such as utilities always overspent and stationery always underspent
Ask what worked, what failed, and which controls were weak
Write the lessons and use them to set **more realistic** budget lines, assumptions and phasing next year

blocks.p: Use evidence in the next budget bid: if utilities were over budget every month, ask for a realistic figure and explain why. Do not simply copy last year's budget and add a percentage.

Keep the records of **why** every spending decision that departed from the plan was made, so it can be explained and checked later. Keep them for the period required by your organisation and audit rules.

ul: explain the roles of the budget holder and the limits of my own authority
phase a budget and plan large purchases against it and against cash
keep a spending log of commitments and actual spending and work out what is still free to commit
reconcile my log with finance's report and find coding errors
calculate variances in J$ and as percentages and say whether they are favourable or adverse
work out the budget to date, an outturn forecast and a reforecast
use a flexed budget to judge performance fairly, and split a variance into price and usage effects
apply an investigation threshold and a RAG rating
find the cause of a variance and take corrective action without harming essential services
explain virement and contingency, and manage an unbudgeted emergency
avoid order splitting, handle gifts and conflicts, and follow procurement rules and value for money
report to my director and involve the team in cost control
review the year and use the findings for the next budget

terms: Variance
The difference between budget and actual.
Favourable / adverse
Under budget on costs / over budget on costs.
Commitments
Orders placed but not yet invoiced or paid.
Phasing
Spreading the yearly budget over months.
Outturn
The expected final result for the year, estimated part-way through.
Reforecast
A new year-end estimate made during the year.
Flexed budget
A budget adjusted to the actual level of activity.
Timing difference
A variance that arises from when a cost is posted and later reverses.
Virement
An approved transfer of budget from one line to another.
Contingency
A small sum set aside for costs that could not be foreseen.
Spending limit
The highest amount a manager may approve alone.
RAG
Red, amber, green rating of each line.
Value for money
The best mix of cost, quality and useful life.
Order splitting
Dividing a purchase to get under an approval limit: a control breach.

c1.title: Portmore parks unit vehicle repairs
c1.text: Mr Garfield Henry manages the parks unit of a municipal corporation in Portmore. His vehicle repairs budget is J$2,400,000 for the year, phased evenly. After five months, finance's report shows actual spending of J$1,150,000. Open purchase orders worth J$300,000 have been raised but not yet invoiced. His own log is up to date and agrees with finance except for one invoice of J$45,000 for tyres for the water-truck, which finance has coded to the parks unit's fuel line.

c2.title: Negril hotel laundry costs
c2.text: A hotel in Negril budgets J$420 of laundry cost for each occupied room. The plan was 3,000 occupied rooms for the quarter, giving a laundry budget of J$1,260,000. The hotel was busier: 3,500 rooms were occupied, and the actual laundry cost was J$1,540,000. The housekeeping manager, Ms Beverley Smith, is asked to explain the overspend.

c3.title: Regional office laptops
c3.text: Mr Delroy Thompson is the budget holder for a ministry's regional office in Cornwall. His spending limit is J$250,000 per purchase. He needs six laptops at J$95,000 each for the field team. A supplier tells him he can 'avoid the paperwork' by ordering two at a time, and offers him a free weekend at a hotel if the office renews a servicing contract. Mr Thompson has also noticed that the office's security contract will be J$300,000 under budget, while the roof of the records room needs urgent repair.

c4.title: Black River depot after floods
c4.text: After heavy flooding, a distribution company's depot in Black River has damaged stock and a leaking roof. Roof repair is estimated at J$1,200,000, which is not in the budget. The depot manager, Mr Paul Gordon, has a contingency line of J$300,000, and the company has an insurance policy that covers storm and flood damage. The company's year ends in March, and it is now February. The depot's stationery line has J$80,000 unspent, and a clerk suggests buying extra stationery so that 'the money is not lost'.

c5.title: Linstead packaging budget
c5.text: A food-processing firm in Linstead buys packaging film from overseas, priced in US dollars. The budget for the year assumed J$150 to US$1. A purchase of US$8,000 was budgeted at J$1,200,000, but the J$ weakened to J$156 to US$1 when it was bought. The production manager, Ms Camille Reid, has given her team leaders a small supplies budget each. This month's finance report shows her packaging line as red, with no explanation.

questions.q: What is the position of the repairs line against the budget to date after five months?
o: J$100,000 over the budget to date, since five months of the year have passed
J$150,000 over the budget to date
J$1,250,000 under budget, since only J$1,150,000 of the J$2,400,000 is spent
J$300,000 over the budget to date, because the open purchase orders must be included
questions.why: Budget to date = 2,400,000 ÷ 12 × 5 = J$1,000,000. Actual J$1,150,000 is J$150,000 (15%) over. Commitments affect what is free to commit, not the variance on actual spending.

questions.q: How much of the repairs budget is still free to commit for the rest of the year?
o: J$1,250,000, which is the yearly budget less actual spending only
J$1,250,000 less the J$45,000 tyre invoice that finance has miscoded
J$650,000, which is the yearly budget less spending and then half of the orders
questions.why: Free to commit = budget − actual − commitments = 2,400,000 − 1,150,000 − 300,000 = J$950,000. Money already promised on orders cannot be spent again.

questions.q: If spending continues at the same monthly rate, by what percentage will the line exceed its yearly budget?
o: 6.25%, since J$150,000 of overspend is 6.25% of J$2,400,000, the whole-year budget
13%, since J$360,000 of overspend is 13% of the J$2,760,000 forecast
0%, since only five months have passed and the unit started the year well
15%, since J$360,000 of overspend is 15% of J$2,400,000
questions.why: J$1,150,000 ÷ 5 = J$230,000 a month; × 12 = J$2,760,000, which is J$360,000 over. 360,000 ÷ 2,400,000 = 15%. Use the budget as the base. Report the forecast now and plan correction.

questions.q: What should Mr Henry do about the J$45,000 tyre invoice that finance has coded to the fuel line?
o: Leave it, because the total across both lines is the same and nothing is lost
Move the J$45,000 in his own log to the fuel line so that his log agrees with finance
Report the coding error to finance in writing and ask for it to be moved
Wait for the year-end review, since coding errors balance out over the year
questions.why: A cost on the wrong line makes both lines wrong, so repairs look better and fuel worse than they are. Tell finance in writing, give the source documents and check the next report.

questions.q: The housekeeping manager is told the overspend is J$280,000. Why is that figure misleading?
o: It ignores GCT, which should be added to the actual figure before comparing
It compares a quarter's actual figure with the budget for a whole year
It compares actual with a budget for 3,000 rooms, when 3,500 rooms were occupied
It uses the budget as the base for the percentage and should use the actual figure
questions.why: The original budget was for 3,000 rooms; more rooms mean more laundry. The flexed budget for 3,500 rooms is J$1,470,000, so the true variance is smaller.

questions.q: What is the flexed budget for laundry, and the variance against it?
o: J$1,470,000, with a variance of J$70,000 favourable
J$1,470,000, with a variance of J$70,000 adverse
J$1,260,000, with a variance of J$280,000 adverse
J$1,540,000, with a variance of J$0 because activity rose
questions.why: 3,500 × J$420 = J$1,470,000. Actual J$1,540,000 is J$70,000 above the flexed budget, so it is adverse (about 4.8%). The extra is still a real overspend to explain, though smaller than it first looks.

questions.q: The actual laundry cost per occupied room was J$440. What does this show?
o: The price or usage per room is above the budgeted J$420, so she should find out why
Laundry costs are fully under control, since the cost per room is close to the budgeted figure
The hotel should lower the number of occupied rooms to reduce laundry cost
The hotel was inefficient because the number of rooms was above the plan
questions.why: J$1,540,000 ÷ 3,500 = J$440 per room, J$20 (about 4.8%) above the allowance. That is the real overspend, and she should check price rises, wastage, rewashing or loss.

questions.q: Which action best uses the variance analysis to help the hotel next year?
o: Raise the laundry budget by a fixed percentage for all rooms whatever the occupancy
Remove laundry from the department's budget and charge it to the front office
Set the laundry budget at the level spent this quarter and stop flexing it
Budget laundry as a rate per occupied room and flex it each month to actual occupancy
questions.why: Laundry varies with occupancy, so a rate per occupied room, flexed monthly, shows whether performance is good or bad. A fixed sum cannot do that.

questions.q: Mr Thompson's limit is J$250,000 and the six laptops cost J$570,000 in total. What should he do?
o: Order two laptops at a time, because each order is within his own limit
Buy three now and three after the end of the month, with a separate purchase order
Ask the supplier to invoice each laptop separately, and so avoid a delay
Send the purchase for approval to the manager whose limit covers J$570,000, with quotes
questions.why: Splitting one purchase to stay under a limit is a control breach. The whole purchase of J$570,000 must be approved by someone whose limit covers it, after quotes.

questions.q: What should Mr Thompson do about the offer of a free hotel weekend?
o: Accept the weekend but pay for the family's meals from his own pocket
Accept it, because the offer is made to the whole office and not just to him
Decline the offer and report it under the gifts policy
Decline, but say nothing, since nothing has been accepted
questions.why: A gift linked to a contract renewal could look like an inducement. Declining and reporting protects the office and shows the supplier that decisions are made on merit.

questions.q: He wants to use the J$300,000 expected saving on the security contract for the urgent roof repair. What is required?
o: Nothing, as long as the total spending of the office stays within the budget
An approved virement under the office's financial rules, with the reason recorded
A verbal agreement from the supplier of the roof repair that payment can wait
The repair should be coded to the security line so that the lines balance
questions.why: A virement is an approved transfer between budget lines. Spending a saving on another purpose without approval breaches financial rules, even if the total stays within the budget.

questions.q: Which approach best meets the public procurement rules for the laptops?
o: Get written quotes from several suppliers, choose on value for money and record why
Buy from the supplier who offered the gift, since he has already given a price
Choose the lowest price, with no check on quality, support or life
Buy from the supplier used by the regional office last year, without quotations
questions.why: Public procurement must be fair, open, recorded and give value for money. Quotes from several suppliers, judged on cost, quality and support, with reasons recorded, meet that.

questions.q: What should Mr Gordon do first after the flooding?
o: Make the site safe, then record the damage with photographs
Order the roofing material at once from the supplier who is quickest
Wait for the year-end review to see whether there is any budget for it
Move the damaged stock off the books so that the loss is not visible
questions.why: Safety comes first. Records of the damage are then needed for the insurance claim and for approvals. Spending before approval and records can lose both cover and trust.

questions.q: The roof repair costs J$1,200,000 and the contingency is J$300,000. How should the cost be financed?
o: Charge the whole J$1,200,000 to the contingency line and ask finance to cover the difference later
Pay it from the stationery line and the other small lines, without approval, since it is an emergency
Delay the repair until the next financial year so that no unbudgeted cost is incurred
Claim on the insurance, and seek approval to use the contingency for the balance
questions.why: Report to finance, check what the insurance covers, and then use contingency and any approved virement or supplementary funding under the rules. Do not use unapproved transfers.

questions.q: A clerk suggests buying J$80,000 of extra stationery before March so that the money is not lost. What should Mr Gordon do?
o: Agree, since the stationery will be used next year and the budget will then be lower
Agree, but code the purchase to the repairs line to reduce the repair cost
Decline, spend only on real needs and report the saving
Buy it but ask the supplier to invoice it in April
questions.why: Buying what is not needed wastes money and damages trust. Report the saving. If funds are needed for the roof, ask for approval to transfer the saving through a virement, with reasons.

questions.q: Which fact most helps the case for an approved supplementary allocation or virement?
o: The depot manager's own view that the repair is urgent and that the flooding was very severe
Dated photographs and a written estimate of the damage and cost
A verbal promise from the contractor that the price for the work will not change before March
The depot's record of spending below budget on every line in each of the previous three years
questions.why: Approvers and insurers need evidence. Dated photographs and written estimates support the amount and the need, whereas opinions and promises do not.

questions.q: What is the variance on the US$8,000 purchase, and what caused it?
o: J$48,000 favourable, since the J$ now buys more US dollars of film
J$48,000 adverse, caused by the exchange rate, not by quantity
J$8,000 adverse, since the exchange rate differs by 6 on each US dollar
J$96,000 adverse, as the purchase of US$8,000 is doubled by the weaker rate
questions.why: 8,000 × 156 = J$1,248,000, against 8,000 × 150 = J$1,200,000. The J$48,000 (4%) adverse is a price effect from the exchange rate, mostly outside the manager's control.

questions.q: The packaging line is red with no explanation. What should Ms Reid add to her report?
o: The cause, the effect, the action to be taken, who is responsible and by when
A second red mark on the other lines to show they are also at risk
A request that finance changes the colour to amber because the cause is external
Nothing, because the colour already tells the director what the problem is
questions.why: A rating without an explanation does not help the reader. Every red line should show cause, effect and action, with an owner and date, and say what is within the manager's control.

questions.q: Ms Reid delegates small supplies budgets to her team leaders. Which arrangement is most sound?
o: Give each leader the money and ask for the receipts at the end of the year
Give no limit, because the leaders know their needs best
Give the leaders access to the full budget, so that they can transfer between lines
Give clear limits, a simple log and regular check-ins, while she remains accountable
questions.why: Delegation helps cost awareness and speed, but the manager remains accountable. Limits, simple records and regular review reduce the risk of mistakes.

questions.q: How could the firm reduce this kind of exchange-rate effect on future packaging orders?
o: Cut the packaging budget by the same percentage as this year's overspend
Ask the overseas supplier to lower its US$ price whenever the J$ weakens
Ask the supplier to quote in J$, or place orders earlier when the rate suits
Charge the extra cost to the production wages line so the film line stays green
questions.why: Costs priced in a foreign currency move with the exchange rate. Quoting in J$ or buying ahead (within cash limits) reduces the risk. Moving costs to another line only hides it.
